Each face gets 100 N. The defined force is applied uniformly to the selected objects, so a 200 N load on two faces of equal area loads each face uniformly with 100 N.
The FreeCAD FEM ConstraintForce feature uses the *CLOAD card in CalculiX.

FreeCAD uses Gmsh as the default mesher to create a FEM Mesh. Depending on your OS and installation, Gmsh may be bundled with FreeCAD; otherwise install it separately and set its path in Edit → Preferences → FEM → Gmsh.
If Gmsh is not bundled with your FreeCAD installation, install it separately and then set the path to gmsh.exe in the menu Edit → Preferences → FEM → Gmsh.

Try these strategies: (1) Set Data Second Order Linear to true but keep Data Element Order at 2nd. (2) Set Data Element Order to 1st. (3) Use a smaller element size by reducing Data Characteristic Length Max. If solver ccxtools is used and the run button is used (not the task panel), the nodes of nonpositive jacobian elements will be green.
Elmer does not support Netgen meshes, according to the FEM MeshNetgenFromShape description.

Run the single command `ccx` in the terminal. If the solver is installed correctly, it responds with a simple usage message: "Usage: CalculiX.exe -i jobname". You should also make sure the FEM Workbench can find the binary via Edit → Preferences → FEM → CalculiX → Search in known binary directories (untick it and give the correct path if you compiled the solver yourself).

The original framework Solver CalculiX Standard is preferred because it contains extra checks, e.g. showing the elements with nonpositive Jacobian which might cause solution difficulties. The new framework (shared with the Elmer and Z88 solvers) keeps its code hidden from the user.

In FreeCAD 0.21 and below, the self-weight constraint uses a fixed gravity acceleration of 9.81 m/s^2 (written as 9810 mm/s^2 in the CalculiX .inp file). It can only be changed by manually editing the .inp file.
If checked, multiple *.inp files are written and the main input deck uses the *INCLUDE keywords to reference the other ones. If unchecked, a single large *.inp file is written.

The PartDesign Pad tool extrudes a sketch or a face along a straight path. You select a single sketch or one or more faces from the Body and invoke it from the Pad button or via Part Design → Additive Features → Pad, then set the parameters in the task panel.
A positive taper angle makes the outer pad border get wider as the pad extends in the extrusion direction. The Taper angle option is only available if Type is Dimension.
For technical reasons, a Through All pocket is actually 10 meters deep. It extends up to the last face of the support it encounters in its direction. For deeper pockets, use the type Dimension.

The Tip is the PartDesign Feature exposed outside the Body: if another tool (e.g. Part SimpleCopy or Part Cut) needs the Body's shape, it uses the shape of the Tip. It is the final representation of the Body as if the parametric history didn't exist. By default, the Tip is automatically set to the last feature created in the Body. It can be changed to an intermediate feature via the Tree View context menu (Set Tip) or the Body's Data Tip property.
The PartDesign Hole feature can create countersink, counterbore, and straight holes. Threading, size and fit can also be set.

Edge numbers are not completely stable. If you apply fillets or chamfers before the main design work of the solid body is finished, edges could change names (the topological naming problem) and the filleted edges would likely become invalid. Some protection exists when the Data Use All Edges property is true, because then all edges of the base object are used and there is no dependence on individual edge names.

Differences listed in the docs:
- Part Extrude always creates a standalone shape; PartDesign Pad fuses the extrusion result to the rest of the Body.
- Part Extrude can be placed anywhere in the model tree; PartDesign Pad can only be placed inside a PartDesign Body.
- Part Extrude can extrude any object with Part geometry (OpenCASCADE shape) except solids and CompSolids; it can also extrude individual faces of other objects.
- PartDesign Pad only accepts a Sketch or faces of PartDesign objects as a profile.

Booleans are performed by the OpenCASCADE Technology (OCCT) kernel, which sometimes has problems producing results when the input objects share an edge or a face (coplanarity). Even if the first boolean succeeds, later nested operations may fail, so the real problem can be in an older operation. To avoid this, make the shapes intersect clearly (one protrudes or is larger than the other), and use Part CheckGeometry to inspect all objects when troubleshooting.

The Sketcher ConstrainLock tool (Lock Position) applies horizontal dimension and vertical dimension constraints to points. If a single point is selected, the constraints reference the sketch origin. If two or more points are selected, they reference the last point in the selection.
An unconstrained line in the Sketcher has 4 degrees of freedom (DoF): it can be moved horizontally or vertically, stretched, and rotated.
If two lines are selected (or a line and the endpoint of another line), the ConstrainTangent tool makes the lines collinear rather than tangent in the usual sense.

Run the installer from the command line with the /S flag: FreeCAD-~.exe /S. Default settings are used for all options. To set a custom installation path, use: FreeCAD-~.exe /S /D=A path to FreeCAD with spaces. A short popup for the corruption check (cyclic redundancy check) still appears by default; it can be disabled with FreeCAD-~.exe /S /NCRC, but this is not recommended because the check ensures the installer was e.g. completely downloaded.

With HomeBrew installed, run in your terminal: `brew install --cask freecad`. To use the latest version available on HomeBrew, run: `brew install freecad`. Issues with the HomeBrew Cask or Formula can be reported to the HomeBrew links given in the docs.

The topological naming problem is a complex CAD modelling issue that stems from how FreeCAD's internal routines handle updates of geometrical shapes created with the OCCT kernel. When the model changes, elements such as edges or vertices may be internally renamed. For example, in TechDraw a dimension measuring a projected edge may break if the 3D model changes, because the vertices may be renamed and the measured edge changes. The problem is not unique to FreeCAD, but most other CAD software has heuristics to reduce its impact. Starting with FreeCAD 0.19 there have been efforts to add such heuristics, and the first stable release with the new naming algorithm is 1.0. The problem most often affects and confuses new users.
The Assembly Workbench uses the open-source Ondsel solver.

Each FreeCAD object has a Data Placement property, which contains the Data Base (position) and Data Rotation (orientation) of the object. It can be manipulated in Python, e.g. box.Placement.Base = sumvec, or via the property editor. The excerpts do not describe deeper internal storage details beyond this.
The Std Measure command gives access to the Unified Measurement Facility, which replaces several previous measurement commands and provides versatile measurement functionality.

For structures, the *BOUNDARY keyword can prescribe temperature, displacements and rotations. The degrees of freedom used are 1–3 (translation in the local x, y, z-direction) and 4 (rotation about the local x-axis, only for nodes belonging to beams or shells), and 5 (rotation about the...; the excerpt is cut off here). Temperature for structures corresponds to degree of freedom 0 or 11, per the uboun.f description.
Temperature is degree of freedom 11 on the *BOUNDARY card (the heat transfer section states this explicitly). The user-subroutine section also mentions "degree of freedom 0 or 11 (i.e. temperature)".

Use the *CLOAD keyword (step keyword), which applies concentrated forces to any node not fixed by a single or multiple point constraint. Data line format, per the example: node, degree of freedom, magnitude, e.g. `*CLOAD` then `1000,3,10.3` applies a force of 10.3 in DOF 3 of node 1000 (global unless a transformation was defined for the node, then local). Optional parameters: OP, AMPLITUDE, TIME DELAY, USER, LOAD CASE, SECTOR, SUBMODEL, STEP, DATA SET and OMEGA0. OP=MOD (default) keeps loads from previous steps (a force on the same node replaces the earlier value; a force on the same node/direction within the same step is added), while OP=NEW removes all previously applied concentrated loads. Example: `*CLOAD,OP=NEW,AMPLITUDE=A1,TIME DELAY=20` followed by `1000,3,10.3`.

According to the *DENSITY documentation, mass density is required for a frequency analysis (*FREQUENCY), for a dynamic analysis (*DYNAMIC or *HEAT TRANSFER), and for a static analysis with gravity loads (GRAV) or centrifugal loads (CENTRIF). The density can be temperature dependent.

A CalculiX material name (the NAME parameter of *MATERIAL) can contain up to 80 characters. For user materials the name must start with a fixed prefix (e.g. "SINGLE CRYSTAL", "COMPRESSION ONLY", "CIARLET EL"), and the remaining characters up to the 80 limit can be freely chosen.

Use the *FREQUENCY step card and put the number of eigenfrequencies on the second line: "*FREQUENCY" followed by "10" requests the 10 lowest eigenfrequencies and corresponding eigenmodes. Results are always stored in jobname.dat. Optionally, the second line can also give a lower and upper frequency range bound. If Coriolis forces matter, *COMPLEX FREQUENCY,CORIOLIS with 10 on the second line does the same, but it must be preceded by a *FREQUENCY step that uses STORAGE=YES.

C3D10 is a 10-node quadratic tetrahedral element. It is a general purpose tetrahedral element with 4 integration points, behaves very well, and is attractive because fully automatic tetrahedral meshers exist (although C3D20R yields still better results for the same number of degrees of freedom).

By default a *STATIC step uses the first solver that has been installed from this list: SGI, PaStiX, PARDISO, SPOOLES and TAUCS. If none of them is installed, the default is the iterative solver (by Rank and Ruecker) that comes with CalculiX. The SOLVER parameter can be used to select a different one.

No special compilation flag is needed. At execution time set the environment variable OMP NUM THREADS (OMP_NUM_THREADS) or CCX NPROC STIFFNESS to the number of cores (default is 1). If both are set, CCX NPROC STIFFNESS takes precedence. CalculiX detects the maximum number of cores automatically via sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_CONF), which you can override with the environment variable NUMBER OF CPUS.

Run a linearized version first: eliminate large deformations (drop NLGEOM), use a linear elastic material, and drop all other nonlinearities such as contact. If the linear version doesn't run, the nonlinear problem won't run either. The linear run also lets you check that boundary conditions are correct (no unrestrained rigid body modes) and that the loading is as intended, and it gives you a feeling for what the solution should look like.
On the *SOLID SECTION card, the parameters ELSET and MATERIAL are required. ORIENTATION and NODAL THICKNESS are optional.
Each *STEP card must at some point be followed by an *END STEP card, which concludes the definition of the step.

The *BUCKLE procedure determines the buckling load of a structure. It solves an eigenvalue problem whose lowest eigenvalue is the scalar by which the load in the buckling step must be multiplied to get the buckling load, so generally only the lowest eigenvalue is needed. Only the stress stiffness due to the buckling load is taken into account, not the large deformation stiffness.
